A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WebAggregator research, despite the changed title and framing. All 24 pages of v1 and 32 pages of v2, including appendices, tables and figures, were readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original fine-tuning results, benchmark evaluations, training-data efficiency experiments and agent trajectory analyses, particularly in Tables 3–5 and Section 4.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds model comparisons, behavioral measurements, correlation analyses, contamination diagnostics and annotated failure trajectories.

M1.justification: The exploration/composition pipeline, operation taxonomy, rejection sampling and SFT procedure remain intact. Appendix B.4 adds an explicit instruction to check the QA by solving it, also reflected in Section 2.2.3, providing a limited refinement of the specified verification procedure. The broader component renaming does not establish a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the same 9,883-task corpus, 159-item test set and evaluations on GAIA-text, WebAggregatorQA, WebWalkerQA and XBench. The latter two already appear in v1 Table 4. GAIA-para in v2 is a derived contamination-analysis control, rather than new agent task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds GPT-5 and removes MiroThinker from the main comparison. Table 2 adds GPT-4.1 and 32B WebDancer/WebSailor comparators to the retained WebWalkerQA/XBench comparisons. Table 3 also adds untuned Qwen3-32B to the reference-access analysis.

E3.justification: v2 adds several diagnostic evaluation designs: GPT-5 classification of 500 sampled steps per model, manual examination of 50 trajectories, logic-type correlations, and contamination analysis using a GAIA paraphrase control and 100,000 cross-dataset pairs. It also changes tool-call density from the percentage of steps using tools to calls per step. These substantially expand the analytical protocols; the retained benchmark experiments are not documented as rerun.

E4.justification: Sections 4.3–4.4 add before/after fine-tuning analyses of reasoning and tool use, composition-type difficulty analysis, and a failure taxonomy. Appendices C–D add contamination diagnostics and three annotated failure trajectories. The 500- and 1,200-sample training-efficiency experiment already existed in v1 and is relocated to v2 Section 3.2.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 7 introduces significance reporting for Phi correlations, distinguishing p < 0.05 from p >= 0.05. v1 has no corresponding reporting. Neither version documents seed-based uncertainty estimates or an increase in repeated runs; pass@3 results already existed in v1.

E6.justification: Shared rows in v1 Table 3 and v2 Table 1 retain their scores. Additions include GPT-5's 60.2/28.9 averages and WebAggregator-Qwen3-32B's 43.5/58.0 on WebWalkerQA/XBench, plus substantial behavioral, correlation, contamination and failure results. MiroThinker's 55.3 GAIA entry is removed. Tool-density values are revised under the changed definition. v2 also reassigns construction percentages to different tool counts despite retaining the distribution figure.

T1.justification: The explicit definition of tool-call density changes from the percentage of steps involving tool use in v1 Section 4.2 to calls per step in v2 Section 4.2. v2 Table 5 distinguishes these two quantities. This is a limited mathematical-definition revision; no new theorem, proof or theoretical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add a central claim that fine-tuning transforms agent behavior by increasing deliberate reasoning and reducing redundant tool use. They strengthen the aggregation challenge into a claim that compositional reasoning is the performance ceiling despite perfect retrieval. v2 also explicitly extends the claimed Claude-3.7-Sonnet match to GAIA, WebWalkerQA and XBench.

C2.justification: v2 introduces substantive interpretations about reasoning versus verbosity, internal synthesis, scaling and tool efficiency, plus explanations involving faulty composition, accumulated errors and ineffective refinement. Its new contamination discussion makes stronger assurances about benchmark overlap. It removes v1's explanation attributing commercial models' advantage largely to multimodal capabilities.

D1.justification: v2 identifies GPT-5 as the thought classifier and Qwen3-Embedding-8B for semantic similarity, and refines the checker prompt. It omits v1's explicit 103-case GAIA count, allowance for two exception retries, and Screenshot/Scroll exclusions during trajectory collection. These omissions reduce documentation without establishing changed settings. The 30-step budget, core prompts and repository links remain.

R1.justification: Section 5 adds a focused discussion of reinforcement-learning credit assignment and test-time self-evolution with newer references. Several earlier citations, including Query2box and OpenWebVoyager, disappear. The central positioning against retrieval-oriented datasets and existing web-agent benchmarks remains.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten around compositional reasoning, and Explore to Evolve and its components are renamed. The analysis narrative is reorganized, training efficiency moves into the results section, and a Limitations section and Appendices C–D are added.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the single-column technical-report layout with two columns, removes the opening performance chart, and adds an introductory task comparison. It combines the resource table and examples into Figure 2, redraws the pipeline, moves the operation table and word cloud into the appendix, and adds behavioral, correlation, contamination and annotated-trajectory displays.

improvement.justification: The added comparisons, behavioral measurements and failure traces provide useful evidence beyond v1. However, v2 invokes perfect retrieval or supplied full context without documenting a corresponding controlled experiment, and claims zero overlap with existing benchmarks from Appendix C's sampled GAIA-only analysis. Its revised exploration percentages also contradict the retained distribution figure. These problems affect the central evidential argument, leaving the net quality direction uncertain despite the useful additions.
